clue.text: BBC boss is fool to seize Ecstasy found in Blowers' trunks

indicators.note: the run of pieces is found inside the word for those who blow, placed within it

parts.note: buglers are people who blow horns, so blowers
DG, the Director-General, heads the BBC

indicators.note: the word is grabs hold of the drug letter, taking it inside

parts.note: taken as written
E is the usual abbreviation for the drug ecstasy
a mug is a gullible fool

explanation.surface: A BBC chief and a fool smuggle drugs inside a cricket commentator's swimming costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blowers' looks like the nickname of commentator Henry Blofeld, but here it is BUGLERS. Budgie smugglers is Australian-born slang for skimpy men's swimming briefs.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang term for tight men's swimming briefs, a kind of swimming trunks.

clue.text: Not e.g. a fry-up of baked beans with beluga? Queen tucks in

definitions.text: Not e.g. a fry-up of baked beans with beluga? Queen tucks in

indicators.note: the royal abbreviation is tucked inside, eating into the dish
says the letters of e.g. a are removed from the pool
a fry-up mixes everything in the pan, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Fussy royalty refusing a posh fry-up of baked beans and caviar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' strips E, G and A from the pool that 'fry-up of' mixes, leaving BUBBLEANDSEAK. Bubble and squeak is a British dish of fried leftover potato and cabbage.
explanation.definitionFit: Bubble and squeak is a fry-up of leftover vegetables, never of beans and caviar.

clue.text: During refurb, Black Lion invests ton for highly-sought-after bed

indicators.note: during means within, so the lion pieces sit inside the refurb phrase

parts.note: to do up a place is to refurbish it
B is short for black, as on pencils

indicators.note: the lion sign encloses, investing itself around, the ton letter

parts.note: Leo is the lion of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A pub called the Black Lion is being renovated with a large investment for a fancy bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invests' puts T in LEO; 'During' puts B + LETO inside DO UP. In darts, the double-20 segment, a bed, is the favourite target.
explanation.definitionFit: In darts, double top is the outer ring segment of the 20, a much-aimed-for bed of the board.

clue.text: Completely freeze, giving address in Clerkenwell?

definitions.meaning: Clerkenwell's London postcode is EC1; the entry's first three letters, read upwards in this down light, spell EC1

explanation.surface: A cold snap so hard it freezes a London neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the entry as an instruction: ICE written up the grid reads EC I, i.e. EC1, the postcode of Clerkenwell, an area of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: To ice up is to become totally covered or blocked with frozen water.

clue.text: Flag of St George? It's what we're taught

parts.note: a standard is a flag or banner
St George is the patron saint of England, so English

explanation.surface: A schoolroom lesson about England's flag.
explanation.walkthrough: The flag of St George is England's red cross on white.
explanation.definitionFit: The accepted form of the language is taught in schools as the correct norm.

clue.text: Shocking cuts raise digit by a point, roughly as predicted

parts.note: to put up is to raise
a toe is a digit of the foot
x is the times sign, as in 3 by 4

indicators.note: the therapy letters cut into the rough version of a point
a rough version of the words a point has its letters jumbled

parts.note: ECT, electroconvulsive therapy, treats by electric shock

explanation.surface: Harsh spending cuts push up the figures by a point, more or less as forecast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' makes PATION from A POINT; ECT 'cuts' it after the P.
explanation.definitionFit: Being up to expectation means meeting the standard that was anticipated.

clue.text: Saw a little chap fishing in the garden

definitions.meaning: a saw is a wise saying, an aphorism or maxim

definitions.text: a little chap fishing in the garden
definitions.meaning: the classic ornamental figure of a small bearded man with a fishing rod beside a pond

explanation.surface: Spotted a small man with a rod in someone's garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' reads as the past of see but is the noun for a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A pithy maxim is one sense; the other is a garden ornament of a dwarf.

clue.text: Work a bit at her enunciation?

definitions.text: Work a bit at her enunciation?

parts.words: Work a bit at her enunciation?
parts.note: Work a bit suggests do little, the surname of the flower girl whose speech is reformed in Pygmalion and My Fair Lady

explanation.surface: A suggestion to someone to practise speaking more clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's heroine Doolittle (do little = work a bit) has her diction worked on by Professor Higgins.
explanation.definitionFit: Doolittle is the cockney heroine of Pygmalion who takes elocution lessons.

clue.text: Perhaps circumflex C, then ec + o: investigate possible solutions

wordplay.reading: C hat, then E, C and O

parts.words: Perhaps circumflex C, then ec + o
parts.note: a circumflex is a hat-shaped accent, so a C wearing one is C hat, sounding like the opening words; the remaining letters give what one can manage

explanation.surface: Reads like a puzzle about accents and letters, ending in a call to try things out.
explanation.walkthrough: A circumflex over a letter is nicknamed a hat, so C hat suggests the opening words.
explanation.definitionFit: To try out what is achievable is to explore the possible ways of solving something.

clue.text: Unsweetened French coffee revolutionising tea? We hear it's true

parts.note: brut describes very dry, unsweetened champagne

indicators.note: revolving the French coffee word turns it round so it reads backwards

parts.note: café is French for coffee

indicators.note: signals that the word tea is only heard, giving the letter with the same sound

parts.note: the drink sounds like the letter T

explanation.surface: A dry French coffee seems to be shaking up tea drinking, if the rumour is true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unsweetened' looks like it describes the coffee, but it is BRUT on its own; 'revolutionising' makes EFAC from CAFE.
explanation.definitionFit: A brute fact is a plain fact that simply holds, with no further explanation.

clue.text: Wanting initially to be green

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the synonym for wanting is kept, the rest cut away

parts.note: owing, falling short, is a sense of wanting
to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: Someone longing to go green, perhaps environmentally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' trims OWING to its first letter, O.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive is a shade of dull yellowish green, so being olive means being a green colour.

clue.text: One floating top new play parts

indicators.note: the shuffled play splits the word for top apart, sitting in the middle

parts.note: a lid is the top of a container

indicators.note: a new version of the word play has its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A cast member, the top of the bill, takes roles in a new play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges PLAY to LYPA, which 'parts' LID into LI...D.
explanation.definitionFit: The broad leaf of a water lily rests on the surface of a pond, so it is something that floats.

clue.text: With no strategy in place, plane trees rot

indicators.note: the word plane is left lacking the strategy word, which is removed

parts.note: a plan is a strategy
the yew and the ash are two trees

explanation.surface: Without any plan in place, the plane trees are left to decay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With no' strips PLAN from PLANE, leaving E. 'Plane' seems to qualify the trees, but it is separate fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean nonsense or humbug, talk not to be taken seriously.

clue.text: When tile falls off for no good reason?

definitions.text: When tile falls off for no good reason?

parts.words: When tile falls off for no good reason?
parts.note: tile is slang for a hat, so a hat being let fall describes the phrase literally, while the idiom means without needing any cause or persuasion

explanation.surface: A roof tile drops off with no obvious cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tile' looks like a roof tile but is old slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means instantly and readily, needing no real cause or prompting.

clue.text: Character appearing in fringe theatre thrice? Thrice

indicators.note: the letters appear inside the phrase fringe theatre, straddling the two words

explanation.surface: An actor appearing three times in a fringe production.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters turn up hidden across 'fringe theatre', again across 'theatre thrice', and again across 'thrice? Thrice': three times, as the clue says.
explanation.definitionFit: Eth is a letter of the Old English and Icelandic alphabets, a written character.

clue.text: Fine theatre job, exquisite

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
an op is an operation, a job done in an operating theatre

explanation.surface: A fine, delicate piece of stage work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exquisite' looks like an adjective but is an old noun for a dandy; 'theatre' is the hospital kind.
explanation.definitionFit: An exquisite, as a noun, is a man overly devoted to fashion, a dandy.

clue.text: Deerstalker perhaps worn by tiddly Irish rector — is he sorry to have put it on?

definitions.text: is he sorry to have put it on?

indicators.note: the hat is worn over the head, so it goes round the other pieces

parts.note: a deerstalker is an example of a hat

indicators.note: tiddly means tipsy, so the word Irish staggers into a new order

explanation.surface: A tipsy Irish clergyman in a deerstalker, perhaps regretting his choice of headgear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tiddly' is British slang for slightly drunk. The garment was worn as a penance, hence the question.
explanation.definitionFit: A coarse penitential garment was worn by the remorseful as a self-punishment.

clue.text: What you must have to fully comprehen viewe backgroun?

definitions.text: What you must have to fully comprehen viewe backgroun?

parts.words: What you must have to fully comprehen viewe backgroun?
parts.note: each truncated word lacks its back letter, so seeing what lies behind, the depth of things, is what is missing from the picture

explanation.surface: A question about what you need to understand a view's background.
explanation.walkthrough: The words with their final letters missing show the backgrounds lost: a reader who cannot perceive what is at the back lacks this faculty.
explanation.definitionFit: The visual ability to judge distance and see things in three dimensions, so as to see the background.

clue.text: Clam: water shifts one into hold

indicators.note: a letter of the water word is shifted from its place to another
says where the moved letter goes: into the word for hold

parts.note: aqua is Latin for water
to hug is to hold
a is one, as in a single

explanation.surface: A clam: water moves one into the ship's hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening A of AQUA moves into HUG, giving QUA + HAUG. A quahaug is a hard-shelled North American clam.
explanation.definitionFit: The quahaug is a species of edible hard-shelled clam from the Atlantic coast of North America.

clue.text: Greek consumed by past grief

indicators.note: the Greek letters are swallowed up inside the past word

parts.note: ago means in the past

explanation.surface: A Greek eaten up by old sorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grief' is the informal sense of trouble and hassle, not sorrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is British slang for trouble or hassle, which is what grief means informally.

clue.text: Hollow spaces in European trains

indicators.note: the letters sit in the words European trains, across the gap

explanation.surface: Cavernous spaces aboard continental railway carriages.
explanation.definitionFit: Antra is the plural of antrum, an anatomical cavity or sinus.

clue.text: Unfortunate case in which tip for memorising assists

definitions.text: Unfortunate case in which tip for memorising assists

indicators.note: an unfortunate arrangement of the letters means they are shuffled
the tip of memorising is its first letter

explanation.surface: A sad case of someone who needs memory aids to get by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunate' shuffles CASE IN plus M, the 'tip for' memorising. Read whole, the clue describes the answer: someone who has lost their memory.
explanation.definitionFit: A person suffering memory loss, an unfortunate case helped by mnemonic tricks.

clue.text: Nervously go in a wood

indicators.note: nervous movement is jittery, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Timidly entering a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wood' is not a forest but a timber; ngaio is a New Zealand tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Ngaio is a New Zealand tree yielding a light timber.

clue.text: Going in the appropriate direction, Joe's joined the rowing crew

indicators.note: rowers face backwards as they travel, so the appropriate way for a rowing word is backwards
the soldier joins by entering the word the, sitting inside it

parts.note: taken as written
GI Joe: a GI is an American soldier; the 's stands for has

explanation.surface: Joe has signed up for the rowing team, heading the right way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going in the appropriate direction' means backwards, since oarsmen sit facing the stern; it turns THGIE round.
explanation.definitionFit: An eight is a racing boat rowed by eight oarsmen, and its crew.

clue.text: I'm the champion Frenchman who directed retrospective parody

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: looking back, so the pieces are read in reverse order

parts.note: number one, No. 1, written NO I
Jacques Tati, the French film director of Monsieur Hulot

explanation.surface: A boast: I'm the champion French director who made a looking-back parody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retrospective' turns NO I TATI into ITATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A parody is a mocking copy, an imitation of a style or work.

clue.text: Fox won't go on ark with fly, I will

definitions.text: Fox won't go on ark with fly, I will

indicators.note: to fly is to move about swiftly, so these letters fly into a new order

explanation.surface: A cunning fox refuses to board Noah's ark, but a fly will.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fly' rearranges WONT GO ON ARK WITH. Read whole, the fox is wise and streetwise: it knows what is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: To be shrewd and experienced, as a crafty fox or a fly person is.
